payload.unsafe_pattern: recursive chmod (execa 'chmod -R a+rX' or equivalent) applied to a directory tree that also holds files intentionally created at 0o600 for sensitive audit/token content
payload.consequence: sensitive audit/token log files become world-readable, an information-disclosure defect
payload.mechanical_correction: scope chmod to the top-level directory and its direct files only, or create sensitive files with restrictive mode via fs.openSync+fchmodSync rather than relying on a later broad chmod pass

payload.unsafe_pattern: Adding behavioral/table-driven assertions for a re-exported function's actual logic (e.g. parseDifcProxyHost host/port parsing, scheme stripping, IPv6 handling, invalid-port errors; filterCapDrop capability bounding-set filtering) directly into a barrel re-export smoke-test file such as src/docker-manager.test.ts, whose file-header comment states it verifies only that the barrel 're-exports every expected symbol and that each symbol has the expected shape (function)...without duplicating the underlying module tests.' The real function already has a dedicated, more complete behavioral suite elsewhere (src/docker-manager-host-config.test.ts for parseDifcProxyHost; src/capability-filter.ts's own test file for filterCapDrop).
payload.consequence: The new assertions pass (the barrel re-export makes them trivially correct) but duplicate coverage already provided by the dedicated module test file, bloat an intentionally symbol-shape-only barrel smoke-test file, and contradict its documented purpose. A human maintainer must manually revert the addition every time, producing a recurring low-value diff and review burden; this happened identically three times from the same automated Test Coverage Improver workflow.
payload.mechanical_correction: When adding coverage for a function, first check whether it already has a behavioral test file for its defining module (e.g. via existing `<module>.test.ts` or `<module>-host-config.test.ts` conventions) before adding assertions to a barrel/re-export test file. If the barrel file's header comment states it checks re-export shape only, confine additions there to `typeof x === 'function'`-style shape checks and add real behavioral assertions to the defining module's own test file instead.

payload.unsafe_pattern: Calling `mount(tools, ['--bind', source, destination])` to bind a source under an already-privatized root (made private via a prior `mount --make-private <root>`) onto a `destination` path that lives OUTSIDE that privatized root (e.g. an invocation export directory under a separate shared `invocationsDir`), without also running `mount --make-private <destination>` on that specific bind result before using it. Privatizing the root/source does not privatize a separate destination mount point that is still covered by a shared ancestor mount.
payload.consequence: Per Linux shared-subtree semantics, binding a private source onto a shared destination mount point creates a shared clone at the destination, even though the source was private. The resulting mount silently remains shared propagation, which can leak mount events/visibility across namespaces and defeat the isolation the privatization was meant to guarantee for enclave/VM storage. This was the confirmed root cause of two consecutive live environment-probe failures (`storage-mount-propagation`) in this repository's Cloud Hypervisor enclave storage setup.
payload.mechanical_correction: After every `mount --bind <source> <destination>` where `destination` is not itself inside a path that was just privatized, immediately run `mount --make-private <destination>` (non-recursive, scoped to exactly that mount) and then verify via `/proc/self/mountinfo` that the resulting entry shows private propagation before trusting the mount. Do this for each distinct bind destination separately; privatizing an ancestor/source does not substitute for privatizing the specific destination mount.

evidence.title: fix: isolate enclave allocation mount propagation
evidence.detail: Root cause: 'the allocation root and artifact parent were overlapping shared peers'. Fix: run `mount --make-private <allocation-root>` before creating any child layout or bind, and verify exactly one private mount-table entry, specifically because nested self-binds inside the allocation were propagating back through overlapping shared views.

evidence.title: fix(enclave): privatize invocation mount beneath shared destination
evidence.detail: Second, distinct occurrence of the same root defect class one probe-release later: 'The private `<allocation>/state` source is bound beneath a shared external invocation destination, so Linux shared-subtree semantics make the new mount shared.' Fix added a dedicated `mount --make-private <invocationHostDir>` immediately after the `--bind` in `mountTmpfs`, plus a post-remount assertion requiring exactly one private entry, because the prior PR's allocation-root privatization did not cover this separate external destination.

syntactic_constructs: mount(tools, ['--bind', source, destination]) call where destination is a distinct path from any previously `--make-private`'d root, with no subsequent `mount(tools, ['--make-private', destination])` call before the mount is relied upon
payload.likely_false_positives: A bind whose destination is itself located inside a path that was already privatized (e.g. binding two paths both under the same already-private allocation root) is safe and should not be flagged; only binds that cross into a separately-rooted, potentially-shared destination are unsafe.
payload.existing_plugin_coverage: None found; this requires tracking prior `mount --make-private` calls against bind destinations across a function, which is repository/domain-specific (Linux mount-namespace shared-subtree semantics) and not modeled by any published generic ESLint rule.
